nameStory: The weeping widow gets its melancholy name from the way moisture beads up and drips from its dark gills, creating the appearance of tears streaming down. This "weeping" effect is most noticeable in humid conditions or after rain, giving these mushrooms their sorrowful, widow-like appearance as they emerge from disturbed soil.
description: The weeping widow is a medium-sized mushroom with a yellowish to grayish cap that can reach about 3 inches across, sometimes showing orange tones in the center. Its dark gills appear to "weep" droplets of moisture, and it sits atop a sturdy stem that can grow up to 5 inches tall. These mushrooms pop up in disturbed areas like gardens, parks, and woodland edges, often appearing after periods of rain.

idTips.label: Gills
idTips.description: Dark gills that often have moisture droplets beading on them, creating a "weeping" effect. The gills are attached to the stem and produce a blackish-brown spore print.

idTips.label: Cap
idTips.description: Yellowish to grayish cap up to 3+ inches wide, sometimes with orangish coloring in the center. The surface feels smooth to slightly sticky when moist.

idTips.label: Stem
idTips.description: Sturdy white to pale stem up to 5 inches tall and about half an inch thick, with a relatively firm texture that doesn't break easily.

idTips.label: Spore Print
idTips.description: Blackish-brown spore print, which you can see by placing the cap gill-side down on white paper overnight.

idTips.label: Smell
idTips.description: Mild, earthy mushroom smell without any strong or unpleasant odors.

habitat: Look for weeping widows in disturbed soil areas throughout New England, including gardens, parks, woodland edges, and areas where the ground has been recently worked. They prefer rich, organic soil and often appear in mulched areas or where leaf litter has been disturbed. You'll commonly find them in both urban and suburban settings as well as forest margins.

seasonality.spring: Early mushrooms may begin appearing in late spring during warm, moist periods, especially in disturbed garden beds.
seasonality.summer: Peak season for weeping widows, with frequent flushes after summer rains. Look for the characteristic moisture droplets on gills during humid mornings.
seasonality.fall: Continue fruiting through early fall, particularly abundant during the rainy season. Often found among falling leaves in parks and gardens.
seasonality.winter: Rarely active during New England winters, though occasional specimens may appear during unusually warm spells.

funFact: The "tears" that give this mushroom its name aren't actually tears at all, but excess water that the mushroom actively pumps out through its gills - it's literally sweating out moisture like a tiny biological air conditioner!
confusionNotes: Weeping widows can be confused with other dark-gilled mushrooms like certain Psathyrella species, but the telltale "weeping" droplets on the gills and the yellowish cap colors help distinguish them. Remember: if the gills aren't visibly moist or beaded with droplets, you're probably looking at something else.
contextualKnowledge: While some sources list this as edible, many people report stomach upset after eating weeping widows, and their close relatives in the brittlestem family can be difficult to distinguish. The common name "widow" also reflects the traditional association of mushrooms with danger - widows being symbols of loss in folklore.
compareHints: As the only Lacrymaria species commonly found in New England, weeping widows are most similar to brittlestems (Psathyrella species) in the same family. However, weeping widows are generally more robust with thicker stems and consistently show the moisture-beading behavior on their gills, while brittlestems tend to be more fragile and don't typically "weep" as noticeably.
